title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction: Euler is setting up the equation of motion of a vibrating elastic lamina (cantilever) clamped in a wall at the portion Aa, with free end F. On the previous page he replaced the motion by a statics problem using d'Alembert's principle. Each element at Y is loaded with the reversed inertial force YV = p dx = (K dx/2bk)(∂²y/∂t²). Here K/2bk is Euler's mass-per-length factor in his gravitational units. These reversed forces must be in equilibrium with two unknown clamping forces applied at A and a; together these two forces can take up any resultant force and couple. Cut the lamina at an arbitrary point Y. The free portion FY carries only the elementary inertial forces, while AY also carries the unknown wall forces. It therefore suffices to consider FY. The moment about Y of the forces on FY is what maintains the curvature at Y: without it, YF would straighten. So this moment must equal the elastic moment defined earlier, K cc times the curvature, i.e. Kcc·∂²y/∂x² in the small-deflection approximation. Section VIII begins computing that moment by freezing Y and letting a variable point run from F to Y. The next page completes this: M(x) = ∫dx∫p dx = (K/2bk)∫dx∫dx ∂²y/∂t², with both integrals vanishing at the free end x=0. Setting M = Kcc·y_xx and differentiating twice gives c²·y_xxxx proportional to −y_tt. In modern terms this is the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation EI y'''' + ρA y_tt = 0, together with the free-end conditions y''=y'''=0.
errors: The elastic moment is printed as K cc (ddy/dt²); it should be K cc (ddy/dx²), i.e. curvature in the space variable. This is a misprint, either in the original or in the transcription; the scan appears to show dt² as well. Euler's subsequent use requires dx².
'portioni B Y' should presumably read 'portioni F Y': the free portion whose forces are being summed. B is the foot of the abscissa origin under F, so the slip is harmless.
Implicit small-deflection assumptions: inertial forces taken perpendicular to the axis, and curvature approximated by y''.

ideas.what: Reduction of the vibration problem to statics by applying reversed inertial forces (d'Alembert's principle) and balancing them against unknown clamping forces at the wall
ideas.usually_credited_to: d'Alembert (1743); used by Euler and Daniel Bernoulli
ideas.where_published: Euler's earlier work on the vibrations of elastic laminae (e.g. the 1744 Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I) and several later papers on beams and chains

ideas.what: Bending moment at a section equals the moment about that section of the loads on the free part, and equals stiffness times curvature
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Bernoulli moment–curvature law; method of sections
ideas.where_published: Euler 1744 Additamentum de curvis elasticis; Daniel Bernoulli and Euler correspondence; Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies

ideas.what: Moment of the distributed load on the free portion written as a double integral vanishing at the free end
ideas.modern_name: Shear/moment integration with free-end boundary conditions M=Q=0
ideas.where_published: Euler's 1735–1744 work on transverse beam vibrations; Truesdell 1960

deep.surprise_reason: Standard derivation of the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation via d'Alembert's principle and the moment of inertial forces on the free segment. This was well known from Euler's earlier work and is thoroughly covered by Truesdell. Nothing new on this page.
transcription_corrections: 'K cc (ddy/dt²)' for the elastic moment should mathematically be 'K cc (ddy/dx²)'; the print appears to have dt², which should be flagged as a misprint.
'portioni B Y' likely intended as 'F Y' (possibly an original misprint).
